question.leadin: Name some World War II leaders.
question.text: This leader coined the term "iron curtain" to describe a barrier between western and eastern Europe and gave his famous "this was their finest hour" speech prior to the Battle of Britain.
question.clue: Clement Attlee replaced this man at the Potsdam Conference after the Conservatives were voted out in July 1945.

swap.text: While returning from the Third Crusade, this king of England was captured and held for ransom by Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV.
swap.answerHtml: Richard I [or Richard the Lionheart; or Richard Coeur de Lion; prompt on “Richard” alone]
swap.clue: He offended Leopold V, the Duke of Austria, after one campaign, leading to his capture, but he was later found by his minstrel Blondel.

question.leadin: This leader crushed the Scots in the Battle of Worcester, a victory which caused Charles II to flee to France.
question.text: Name this Lord Protector of the England, who participated in the English Civil War.
question.clue: The historian John Morrill called this man a "proto-fascist" for his actions at Drogheda and Wexford, after which 50,000 Irish people were deported.

swap.text: At the end of the War of Spanish Secession, Britain gained this overseas possession on the Southern coast of Spain. Its namesake Rock is one of the Pillars of Hercules.
swap.clue: This was the region in which John Lennon and Yoko Ono were married.

question.leadin: He translated St. Augustine's Soliloquies into English.
question.text: Name this ruler of Wessex, the first to take the name of "King of the Anglo-Saxons."
question.clue: He collected his law code in the Doom Book, and he signed the Treaty of Wedmore, which established the borders of the Danelaw.

swap.leadin: World War I is known for its U-Boat attacks and trench warfare, but the war did have one major surface engagement at sea.
swap.text: Over 250 British and German ships fought in this naval battle that, while technically indecisive, left the British in control of the North Sea.
swap.clue: The ironically named (+) Invincible was sunk during this battle, which included a phase called the Run to the South.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the history of internet development.
question.text: Packet switching was pioneered in this country after Donald Davies developed the NPL network. Early computer scientists in this country cracked the Enigma machine.
question.clue: The architect of this country's 1909 "People's Budget" represented it at the Versailles Peace Conference.

swap.leadin: Answer the following questions about a naval fleet commanded by the duke of Medonia Sodenia.
swap.text: This vice admiral under Lord Howard during the English defeat of the Armada pre-emptively shelled the port cities of Cadiz and Corunna in 1587. He circumnavigated the world between 1577 and 1580.
swap.clue: The mojito was invented during this man's victory at Cartagena de Indias, which happened before he evacuated the original Roanoke colony.

question.text: This member of the earlier Hohenstaufen family succeeded Frederick Barbarossa and gained control of Sicily by marrying Constance I. An English king of this name and number founded Eton College and faced Jack Cade's Revolt.
question.clue: This king was deposed and fled to Scotland following the Battle of Towton.

swap.text: According to legend, this British King created the order in 1348 after picking up the Countess of Salisbury's garter.
swap.clue: Under this king, the Statute of Laborers was introduced as an attempt to keep wages low despite major population loss caused by the Black Death.

question.text: The West Port murders were carried out by these two men in Edinburgh in 1828, paving the way for the 1832 Anatomy Act regulating the body trade.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about all the cool shit you can find in the Salisbury Museum.
swap.text: The museum displays the skeleton of a Bronze Age man that was discovered in Avebury in a grave that also contained sixteen flint examples of these objects, which were also often made from chert or obsidian.
swap.answerHtml: arrowheads [or broadheads] (the skeleton was called the Amesbury Archer)
swap.clue: To counter mail armor, this weapon's broadhead variety was gradually replaced by its bodkin variant. Historians debate over whether the Bayeux Tapestry shows Harold Godwinson being felled by this weapon.

question.text: One of Brunel's engineering feats was a bridge named for and opened by this person across the River Tamar. Model cottages named for this person were featured at the Great Exhibition, which this person was responsible for organizing.
question.answer: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
question.clue: As chief organizer of the Great Exhibition, this person commissioned Charles Fox and Joseph Paxton to create a building known as the "Crystal Palace."

swap.text: Corporal punishment was eventually banned in all schools under this Prime Minister, who, earlier on, claimed his top three priorities were "education, education, and education." This man coined the term "New Labour."
swap.clue: This man and Bertie Ahern signed the Good Friday Agreement less than a year into his premiership.

question.leadin: This person's life is attested to in part by four separate wills made from 1394 to 1416, and The Book of Margery Kempe describes a visit regarding their revelations.
question.text: Name this fourteenth-century anchoress and author of the Showings.
question.answerHtml: Julian of Norwich [or Juliana of Norwich; accept Lady Juliana, Dame Juliana or Mother Juliana; prompt on Julian or Juliana alone]

swap.text: This Labour PM served nonconsecutive terms in the 1960s and 70s. He avoided the Vietnam War and opposed Enoch Powell's "Rivers of Blood speech."
swap.clue: This man who was succeeded as UK Prime Minister by James Callaghan.

question.leadin: The leaders of this rebellion, Charles Neville and Thomas Percy, captured the city of Durham and held a Catholic mass after their initial victory.
question.text: Name this attempt to replace the ruling monarch with Mary, Queen of Scots, due to questions surrounding the legitimacy of the marriage of Anne Boleyn ("buh-LIN"). Pius V supported this rebellion by issuing the papal bull Regnans in Excelsis.
question.answerHtml: Rising of the North [or the Revolt of the Northern Earls or the Northern Rebellion]
question.clue: This aristocratic rebellion of 1569, led by Charles Neville and Thomas Percy, aimed to replace Elizabeth I with her cousin Mary, Queen of Scots. It captured Durham, but was put down after failing to gather popular support.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about quotes often mis-attributed to a politician.
swap.text: In an apocryphal story, Churchill told this woman "If I were married to you, I'd put poison in your coffee," to which she replied "If I were married to you, I'd drink it." She was the first woman to sit in the British parliament, though her Nazi sympathies got her into trouble in the 1940s.
swap.clue: This woman, the first to take her parliamentary seat in the House of Commons. This woman founded the Cliveden Set, a club of Nazi sympathizers that pushed for appeasement.

question.leadin: The slang and code of miners of this ethnicity in towns like Real del Monte is thought to be a major influence on albur, a form of Mexican wordplay featuring double entendres.
question.text: Name this ethnicity of the miners who founded Mexico's oldest football club in Pachuca. Emigrants of this ethnicity were often nicknamed "cousin Jacks" when working in areas like South Australia's Copper Coast and Michigan's Upper Peninsula.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about a European custom, FTP each.
swap.text: According to this rule inheritance preference was granted to daughters of a first marriage over sons of subsequent marriages. Louis XIV attempted to invoke it to gain the Spanish Netherlands in starting a namesake war in 1667.
swap.clue: This procedure, which occurred for Wales in 1997, leading to the creation of the Senedd ("SEN-eth").
